elements.element: Customer may terminate the Agreement or an Order Form for convenience.
elements.evidence: Rendered 3.4: "Customer may terminate this Agreement (including all Service Option Attachments) or any Service Option Attachment ... for convenience at any time by: a. providing at least thirty (30) days' prior written notice to IBM". The element is disjunctive and Agreement-level convenience termination is expressly granted; Service Option Attachments are this contract's order-level documents (referenced in the Order Forms per the resolved definition), so document-level partial exit is also preserved. The prerequisite-attachment carve-out is pre-existing language and does not negate the right.

elements.element: Customer's convenience termination requires no more than 30 days' written notice.
elements.evidence: The month-end restriction was replaced with "for convenience at any time" and the notice changed from "at least one month's" to "at least thirty (30) days' prior written notice". With the calendar-month-end trigger removed, the effective date is now a straight 30 days from notice, so nothing pushes the exit beyond 30 days.

elements.element: Vendor refunds prepaid fees pro rata after Customer's convenience termination.
elements.evidence: Added sentence: "In the event of a termination by Customer for convenience under this Section 3.4, IBM will refund to Customer, pro rata, any prepaid charges for the period after the effective date of termination." The refund is expressly pro rata (not merely period-based), is owed by Vendor, and is triggered by Customer's 3.4 convenience termination.

elements.element: Vendor has no right to terminate for convenience during a committed term.
elements.evidence: Retained 3.3 gives IBM a mid-term exit only "for material breach of this Agreement by the other upon written notice" with a cure period; no clause in the operative text confers a Vendor no-cause exit. The only other IBM exit identified is the 90-day non-renewal notice in 3.2, which under the rule boundaries is assessed under RENEWAL as natural-term non-renewal, not as mid-term termination for convenience. Element already met; no edit required.

elements.element: Customer may terminate for convenience on 60 to 90 days' notice.
elements.evidence: Rendered notice is "at least thirty (30) days'", below the 60–90 day fallback band. (This is a Customer-favourable shortfall and is irrelevant because the preferred level is complete.)

elements.element: Any early-termination fee is capped at three months of fees.
elements.evidence: 3.4(b) is retained verbatim and uncapped: "paying the applicable early termination charges, if any, specified in Attachment A and applicable Service Option Attachments." No three-months-of-charges ceiling appears in operative language; the cap is only promised in the rationale as a fallback trade.

elements.element: Vendor may terminate for convenience only at the end of a term.
elements.evidence: Condition satisfied a fortiori: IBM has no convenience termination right at all in the operative text (3.3 is breach-only), so there is no Vendor no-cause exit that could occur mid-term.

elements.element: Vendor must give at least 90 days' notice of convenience termination.
elements.evidence: Conditional element whose stated condition does not apply: IBM holds no convenience termination right in the rendered text, so no Vendor convenience-notice period is required.

reasons: Preferred level is complete on the operative text: the four preferred elements are met by three surgical edits plus one already-met element, so the position is position-complete at the preferred level.

The deterministic check "Customer convenience termination present" reporting false is a false negative on substance: the rendered clause reads "Customer may terminate this Agreement ... for convenience at any time by: a. providing at least thirty (30) days' prior written notice to IBM", which plainly grants the right. The other gates (three operations applying, minimality, element coverage) are consistent with the rendered text.

Minimality holds. Only three targeted changes were made — the month-end trigger became "at any time" (needed so the 30-day cap is not extended by up to a further month), "one month's" became "thirty (30) days'" (needed because one month can exceed 30 days), and a single-sentence pro-rata refund was inserted. Favourable retained language survives verbatim: the prerequisite-attachment carve-out, "if any" in 3.4(b), the continuing-performance sentence, and 3.3's bar on IBM recovering 3.4(b) charges after its own breach. No survival tail, expense language, damages categories, or "in whole or in part" surplus was added.

Intent is preserved: the refund sentence uses the same "effective date of termination" anchor, the continuing-performance sentence's reference to the "final termination date" remains coherent, and 3.3's cross-reference to Section 3.4(b) is intact because 3.4(b) was left untouched. No undefined term or dangling reference is created.

Repair note for the fallback path only: to make the fallback level complete the drafter must add an express operative cap in 3.4(b) (e.g. "which charges shall not in the aggregate exceed three (3) months' charges for the terminated Services") and move Customer notice into the 60–90 day band. As drafted the cap exists only in the margin rationale, which does not count as operative language.

Standing exposure to note in the rationale (not a checklist failure): retained 3.4(b) leaves early-termination charges open-ended by reference to Attachment A and the Service Option Attachments. That is not one of the preferred atomic elements, so it cannot be inferred as an omitted element, but it partially offsets the newly added refund and should be flagged commercially.

Severity: the original clause already gave Customer a one-month convenience exit and gave IBM no convenience right at all, so this is well clear of walk-away territory; the live gaps were the month-end delay, the absent refund, and uncapped exit charges. Medium is the proportionate severity.
